reason: Every claim this objective asks for is a claim about words already fixed on a page: which line-ends rhyme with which, and where the poem changes what it is doing. A turn is not an event that happens in time on a screen; it is an interpretive move the reader makes by holding line 9 against line 1 and arguing that something shifted. A scene can only render that by moving quatrain blocks around or by fading in a 'turn here' marker, and both of those make one reading the structure of the diagram - which is exactly what this case rules out when it says the turn is not arbitrary and that there is no single correct emotional reading. Motion also competes with the work the learner must actually do, which is close reading and quoting a phrase as evidence. The material is static text that needs to stay visible all at once so the learner can move back and forth between the octave and the sestet, and compare two sonnets side by side; a single animated canvas would hide one poem while showing the other. Nothing about rhyme scheme or a volta is a state that changes over time, so animating it would add a false sequence to a judgement about argument.
staticAlternative: Print the Petrarchan sonnet in a wide left column and write the rhyme letters in the right margin at each line end (a b b a a b b a c d e c d e), so the scheme is visible as a shape rather than described. Each learner draws a pencil line where the poem turns and writes the phrase that marks it ('But', 'Yet', 'Then'), with the rule that the line must be supported by a change in what the poem is doing, not by the mere fact that a stanza ended. Then hand out a Shakespearean sonnet of the same length and build the three-column page: Petrarchan text, Shakespearean text, and the bare rhyme skeleton beneath each. One question drives the comparison - in which poem does the rhyme scheme allow the turn earlier, and where does each poet actually put it? Pairs argue for a line number and read the two lines either side aloud, so the claim is testable against the text. Close by asking what the couplet does to the ending in the second poem, and grade the marked line and the quoted evidence, not the emotion the learner reports: two learners may mark the same line and feel opposite things about it.
